alt: Three cards, each with a line diagram: qualification (a level line that steps down at “but”: praise, then a reservation), refinement (a general line that narrows to a sharper one) and reconsideration (a line that loops back: a confident claim, then a changed position).
caption: Qualify, refine or reconsider: a shift shows how the writer’s view develops.

alt: Eight markers of a tone shift: turning transitions, a change of diction, a change in connotation, a change in sentence structure, a change in punctuation, a change of address or pronoun, new imagery and a paragraph break. Below, four steps for describing a shift: locate, name the tone before and after, quote, explain.
caption: Look for a cluster: a turning word plus a change in the words and effect around it.

after: ## A published example: the Declaration of Independence
alt: The Declaration’s two passages side by side: measured and cautious (“Prudence... light and transient causes”), then, after “But”, resolute and accusatory (“abuses and usurpations”, “Despotism”, “right”, “duty”). A line rises sharply at the turn, and a note explains that the shift qualifies the early caution.
caption: “But” turns calm legal language into charged moral language and justifies the break.

after: ## Worked example 1: analysing a shift in a Marlbridge passage
alt: The harbour-front passage split at “Yet”: an admiring description of honey-coloured paving, lantern-shaped lamps and a postcard bay, then the short, blunt “I could not find a single place to sit down”. Notes name the markers and explain that the shift qualifies the praise.
caption: A short, blunt sentence after “Yet” turns admiration into wry criticism.

alt: Three deliberate shifts, each with a marked turn: concession then claim (respectful to firmer), problem then hope (grave to hopeful), and humour then seriousness (light to serious). A note advises marking the turn and avoiding accidental shifts.
caption: A deliberate, clearly marked shift makes writing subtler and more persuasive.
